newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: ARGENTINE ALLIANCE ATTACKED OVER STRIKE SYMPATHY.
newsitem.headline: ARGENTINE ALLIANCE ATTACKED OVER STRIKE SYMPATHY.

text.p: Peronist President Carlos Menem and his union allies attacked Argentina's new Radical Party/Frepaso alliance Monday for expressing sympathy with a general strike planned for Thursday by opposition unions.

Radical and Frepaso leaders, who have united to pose a new challenge to Peronism in October's mid-term elections for Congress and the presidential election in 1999, met the CTA and MTA opposition unions this weekend to discuss the strike.
They emerged saying they sympathized with the motives for the stoppage, but took pains not to appear "strike-happy."
"We are accompanying them politically. The alliance is not a union organization, the roles are different," Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno told reporters Monday.

"Calling a strike is the workers' job. What we are saying is that the workers have more than enough reasons to take whatever action they want because they are in a bad way," said Frepaso leader Sen. Graciela Fernandez Meijide.
But Menem accused the alliance of siding with "a clearly political strike" by "people who don't want Argentina to grow, to progress; who are against the people, against employment."

Menem called their support for the strike -- called to protest labor law reforms and unemployment of 16.1 percent -- "totally inconsistent" with alliance leaders' insistence they would not touch peso parity or undo privatizations.
"Leaders who two weeks before the alliance were against the economic model have suddenly done a somersault in mid-air because they know people back the model," he told local radio.

Despite Menem's attempts to equate the alliance with the economic chaos of the 1980s, when the Radicals ruled under Raul Alfonsin, the business world has welcomed their arrival as proof Argentina's democratic system is fully functioning.
Their choice of former Central Bank chief Jose Luis Machinea, an advisor to the Argentine Industrial Union, as their economic policy chief has been widely praised.
But Menem's ex-Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, running for Congress as an independent, said the alliance's lukewarm support for the strike was contradictory.

"I'm surprised that after pronouncing themselves in favor of an open economy, privatizations and convertibility, they should express support, albeit symbolic, for the CTA and MTA's strike," Cavallo told reporters.

The pro-Menem CGT, the largest union federation which has cut a deal with Menem on labor reform and opposes Thursday's strike, called the alliance "hypocrites and opportunists, for supporting industrial action without any conviction."

"The alliance suports the strike but says it wants to maintain the substance of economic reform, while Machinea goes further still wants to smash collective wage deals, eliminate redundancy pay and totally deregulate healthcare," said CGT spokesman Carlos West Ocampo.
